body: A photo of the Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft, which will conduct low-flying research flights over farmland near Greeley, Colorado, to measure emissions in October 2026. Dynamic Aviation Agricultural emissions represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy more than a dozen sensors to measure ozone, methane, ammonia, particulates, and other pollutants rising from agricultural lands and animal farms and the interaction with the Earth’s atmosphere. The mission is jointly led by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland; Colorado State University; and Boston University.  The Colorado deployment is the first series of flights for the FarmFlux mission. Additional low-altitude research flights are scheduled over farmland in Amarillo, Texas, from late October to early November. title: Long software support matters to smartphone shoppers, poll finds
summary: It's a top priority for almost half of you.
body: Android phones don’t change much from year to year these days; the Galaxy S26 is extremely similar to the Galaxy S25, which was extremely similar to the Galaxy S24, and so on. That means that, assuming you don’t break it, it’s easier than ever to make a device last. Solid hardware only goes so far, though — long software support matters, too. According to a survey Android Authority ‘s been running, almost all of you agree, rating long-lasting software support as a consideration in choosing your phones. In a poll running for the past couple of weeks, we’ve been asking readers whether long software support is a priority in choosing a new phone. There were three options to choose from: “Yes, it’s a top priority;” “Somewhat, but not a dealbreaker;” or “No, I care more about price.” Just shy of 84% of responses indicated that long software support is indeed a priority.

title: Samsung accidentally freezes its smart fridges with a software update
summary: Another reason to think twice about buying a connected appliance.
body: Credit: Samsung TL;DR Samsung has halted a SmartThings update to smart fridges in Korea after some owners reported that their fridges stopped working. Samsung confirmed the issue and said it was taking “emergency measures.” This latest issue once again highlights the risks associated with using connected appliances. There are plenty of smart home appliances on the market, featuring internet connectivity, cross-device integration, and a host of other features. However, there’s no shortage of horror stories about these connected appliances failing. Now, we can add another Samsung smart refrigerator issue to the list. Samsung has stopped rolling out a SmartThings update to its smart refrigerators in Korea after some owners reported major issues, ZDNET Korea reports. More specifically, many users on Samsung’s Korea Community forum report that their fridges completely stopped working, resulting in spoiled food. Other issues include the automatic door-opening function not working and the fridge’s internal lights not turning on.

If you rely a lot on Google Meet for your daily minimum dose of human contact, its “Take notes for me” feature is a godsend. Initially introduced for Workspace accounts, the feature was recently made available to regular Google users and has even expanded to real-life meetings and conversations . Now, Google is adding another layer to the feature that makes it even more useful. Google recently announced “Quick notes” as an extension to Take notes for me in Meet. This new feature offers a high-level summary of the meeting’s key highlights based on the discussion and the notes jotted down by the video calling app.
